National Gallery, London. Founded in 1824, the National Gallery preserves one of the world's most comprehensive collections of European painting from the thirteenth to nineteenth centuries. Located in Trafalgar Square, it was Britain's first major public art collection and remains a model for democratic museum access. The museum's founding came about through the purchase of John Julius Angerstein's private collection. It was originally housed in his own house before moving to purpose-built premises designed by William Wilkins in 1838. The collection spans Italian Renaissance masters including Botticelli, Leonardo, and Raphael, as well as Northern European Old Masters like Van Eyck and Bosch. Spanish, French, and British schools are also represented comprehensively. Vermeer's Woman Standing at a Virginals is one of the world's most celebrated paintings and demonstrates the museum's strength in Dutch Golden Age work alongside significant Rembrandt holdings. The gallery also houses Constable's The Hay Wain and Turner's seascapes, both touchstones of British landscape painting. A distinctive feature of the National Gallery is its acquisition policy, which emphasizes diversity and comparative display. Paintings are grouped by artistic relationships rather than strict chronology, encouraging active looking and interpretation. The building's main gallery is a famous Victorian neoclassical space, and the Sainsbury Wing, designed by Venturi Scott Brown and added in 1991, provided Renaissance galleries without overwhelming the original structure. From its founding, the museum offered free admission to permanent collections—a principle maintained and influential on museums globally—making it a pillar of London's cultural identity and a major tourist destination.
